title: Industrial Revolution in depth
examples: What was the biggest change caused by the steam engine?
How did people move to cities during this time?
Can you explain what the factory acts did for workers?

explain.say: Today we are looking at the Industrial Revolution in depth. We will study new inventions and how cities grew.

items: Step 3: Reform Acts (e.g., Laws for Workers)

explain.say: First we look at key inventions that powered the change. The steam engine improved factories greatly. James Watt significantly improved the steam engine's efficiency.
Next we study urbanisation, which is the rapid growth of towns. Many people moved from rural areas to cities for work. Manchester became a very large industrial centre.
Our third point is the Reform Acts, which were laws made to improve life. These acts aimed to control working conditions for children. The Factory Acts limited the hours children could work.

items: Factory Acts | Limited child labour hours

explain.say: Think about a modern supermarket. It needs many workers and a large building. This shows how industry requires people to live near the jobs.
A common mistake is thinking that all industrial growth was positive. People often forget the terrible living conditions in overcrowded slums. This caused major public health issues.

faq.q: Why did people move to cities during the Industrial Revolution?
faq.a: People moved because factories offered work that was needed. Farming often could not support so many people anymore. They were drawn by the promise of factory wages.
asks: Why did people leave the countryside?

faq.q: What was the main impact of the steam engine?
faq.a: The steam engine provided a powerful, reliable source of energy. It allowed factories to be built far from rivers, changing industry forever. It powered machines everywhere.
asks: What was the engine's main use?

faq.q: What was the purpose of the Reform Acts?
faq.a: The Reform Acts were laws passed to improve life for workers. They tried to limit the worst parts of factory life. They aimed to protect children and women.
asks: What did the laws try to fix?

faq.q: Were all the changes from the Industrial Revolution good?
faq.a: No, the changes had both good and bad sides. While some inventions improved life, the working conditions were often very bad at first. Pollution and poor housing were big problems.
asks: Was the revolution good or bad?
What were the downsides of industrialization?

faq.q: What was the difference between rural and urban life then?
faq.a: Rural life was based on farming and was slower paced. Urban life was centered on factories and was much faster and more crowded. The economies were very different.
asks: What was life like in the country?
How did city life compare to farming?

facts: The steam engine was a crucial invention for factories.
Rapid population growth led to overcrowding in cities.
The Factory Acts were attempts to regulate working hours.
Industrialization caused significant pollution in urban areas.

quiz.say: Which invention was vital for powering factories away from water sources?
quiz.why: The steam engine provided portable and powerful energy, allowing factories to build anywhere.

wrong.0: The steam train used the engine, but the engine itself was the fundamental invention.
wrong.2: The power loom was important, but it needed power from another source, like the steam engine.
wrong.3: The cotton gin was for separating seeds, not for powering large factories.

quiz.say: What major problem resulted from rapid, unplanned city growth?
quiz.why: Overcrowding meant that waste and sewage systems could not keep up with the population.

wrong.0: While job competition was high, the immediate physical problem was sanitation and housing.
wrong.1: Food prices were affected by global trade, but the immediate crisis in the city was health-related.
wrong.2: Low wages were a cause, but the visible, immediate crisis was the unsanitary living environment.

quiz.say: The Reform Acts primarily focused on which area of life?
quiz.why: The main goal of these acts was to legally restrict the time children and women spent working.

wrong.0: The acts did not stop factories; they regulated how they operated.
wrong.1: The acts focused on safety and time, not on giving workers ownership of the means of production.
wrong.2: The acts addressed the conditions within the industrial system, not the location of the population.
